title: Stop Arguing Your Case. Start Holding the Question.
author: Colette Molteni and Craig Mattson
summary: Craig Mattson, guest writing for Empathy Elevated, introduces a fourth communication mode for mid-level leaders facing organizational resistance: holding—a deliberate alternative to arguing (marshaling evidence), ghosting (abandoning the effort), or covering (managing perceptions). The central example is Rachel Hennessy, whose webinar idea was dismissed by her CEO and then, a year later, proposed by him as if it were his own. Mattson argues that what Rachel actually did was hold the question in the organizational atmosphere—keeping it alive in conversations, bringing data when appropriate, letting it mature—until the CEO arrived at it independently. Holding requires patience and a willingness to decouple the value of an idea from who receives credit for it.
points: Mid-level leaders facing resistance typically default to three dysfunctional modes: arguing (more evidence), ghosting (abandoning the effort), or covering (managing perceptions).
Holding is a fourth mode: deliberately carrying an important question in the organizational atmosphere—through conversation, data, and patience—until the conditions for action mature.

The Rachel Hennessy case illustrates holding in practice: a year after her webinar idea was dismissed, her CEO proposed the same idea as his own—evidence that the idea had taken root through sustained holding rather than argument.
Evidence-based argument often fails because people in organizations do not behave as rational actors; the problem is usually not the quality of the argument but the readiness of the audience.
Holding requires separating the value of an idea from the credit for it—a discipline that is particularly demanding for leaders whose ideas routinely get attributed to others.
quotes: I'm going to suggest a fourth way instead. I call it holding.
Trying to argue your way to change isn't likely to work. People often don't behave like rational actors.

Ghosting is what happens when leaders realize, often after one or two failed attempts, that the communication challenge is harder than anticipated. Rather than try a third time, the leader finds some way of working around the roadblock or simply accepts the status quo.
Holding is the recognition that some problems and possibilities need to be carried in the organizational atmosphere for a while before anyone can work on them.

What Rachel actually did—without necessarily knowing it—is hold the question of whether a webinar series would be valuable for the organization. She held it in her own mind, she raised it in conversation, she brought data to it when that was appropriate, and she let it develop.
